items.summary: R scripts and aggregate tables that reproduce every number, table and figure in the article What a national health information system measures: a cross-sectional analysis of respiratory syncytial virus records in Bulgaria, 2022–2026 (Folia Medica, manuscript 215603) and its supplementary files. The package contains the reconstruction ledger of the Ministry of Health release of Bulgarian National Health Information System (NHIS) records for ICD-10 J21.0, J12.1, J20.5 and B97.4; exclusion and validation counts; the 110 distinct laboratory result values (109 text strings and the empty text field of numeric results) with their assigned RSV class and the rule that fired; a script that rebuilds the hospitalisation episodes from the released worksheet; annual population denominators at national and district level (National Statistical Institute table 206/649, population on 31 December 2022–2025); the aggregate model input (year × age × sex cases and person-years, with and without Sliven); model output and diagnostics; and the article figures. Aggregate data only. No record-level rows, identifiers or dates of birth are included; the record-level extract can be requested from the Bulgarian Ministry of Health under the Access to Public Information Act. See README.md for the file map, data sources, disclosure control and how to re-run the pipeline. Tables and figures: CC BY 4.0; R scripts: MIT licence.

items.summary: Recent video world models have increasingly adopted 3D memory mechanisms to integrate historical observations into a lightweight and persistent scene representation. This naturally raises a complementary question: if 3D representations can serve as an effective mechanism for memorizing observed scenes, can they also be directly used as the latent space for reconstructing and generating scenes? Motivated by this idea, we represent a scene as a compact and unstructured 3D-anchored latent space (\textbf{SceneAE}). Each latent combines an explicit 3D position with an implicit content feature and is spatially grounded to describe its local scene region, forming a sparse latent point cloud. Unlike conventional video-VAE latents that describe how a scene appears from particular viewpoints, our representation directly describes the scene itself, making it naturally applicable to both reconstruction and generation. For reconstruction, once the scene has been generated, our persistent 3D representation can be projected and decoded into RGB-D observations by different target cameras, without the need to regenerate a video for each new camera trajectory. For generation, we leverage the geometry-content separation to first generate camera-controlled 3D geometry and then synthesize content conditioned on it, reducing camera-appearance entanglement and improving camera controllability. Experiments show that this 3D latent achieves superior generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.
items.title: SceneAE: Scene Generation and Reconstruction in Queryable 3D-Anchored Latent Space

items.summary: Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference. This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training. Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training. Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at $256 \times 256$ resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of $1.19$ among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming.
items.title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?

items.summary: Reducing memory use in large language model (LLM) training is an ongoing challenge. Activation checkpointing saves memory by recomputation, while lossy compression changes the stored activations. The reemergence of sparse $\relu$ and $\relu^2$ activations creates a third opportunity: losslessly compressing the activation cache itself. We present BitSparse, a GPU-resident lossless compression format for sparse activations. Compression and reconstruction run in custom Triton kernels fused into an autograd function, shrinking the activation cache while recovering it exactly for the backward pass. Bfloat16 (BF16) and FP8 activations are supported. Optional sign-bit packing further increases compression up to close to the theoretical limit. We analyze its compression ratio and compare it to the theoretical optimum. BitSparse lowers per-token VRAM by 31\% and 30\% Modded-NanoGPT and Nemotron-H respectively, with overheads of no more than 1\% at practical sequence lengths. Additionally, a new preallocated buffer system avoids host synchronization during training when variable size tensors are allocated.
items.title: BitSparse: Compact Activation Storage for ReLU Feed-Forward Networks

items.summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
items.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention

items.summary: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction
items.title: Latent Compaction with Test-Time Training

items.summary: Background: Long-segment intramedullary cervical cord lesions can present a diagnostic challenge, particularly when imaging findings raise suspicion of an intramedullary neoplasm. Differentiating a syrinx from an intramedullary tumor is important for operative planning, as the surgical strategy may differ substantially. Case presentation: A 43-year-old female presented with a six-month history of progressive cervical pain with radicular symptoms, vertigo, left upper-limb sensory disturbance, and impaired left-hand grip. Neurological examination revealed preserved motor power of 5/5 in all four limbs, normal reflexes, and reduced functional grip in the left hand. MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated a long-segment expansile intramedullary lesion extending from the cervicomedullary junction to C7, without contrast enhancement. The radiological report also described Chiari malformation and syringomyelia. Given the diagnostic uncertainty and progressive symptoms, we performed urgent surgical exploration within two days of admission. We performed a C3–C7 laminoplasty to provide multilevel posterior access while preserving the laminar elements without instrumented fixation. Following durotomy and midline myelotomy, a syrinx was identified, with no obvious intramedullary tumor. Syringotomy and drainage were performed, and adjacent spinal cord tissue was obtained for biopsy. Graft duraplasty and reconstruction of the elevated laminae were completed. The patient had an uncomplicated postoperative course, with relief of pain and vertigo and resolution of sensory symptoms. She was discharged with intact motor power and improved but residual left-hand grip weakness. Follow-up MRI demonstrated cord decompression and drainage of the syrinx. Conclusion: This case illustrates the diagnostic uncertainty that may arise when a long-segment non-enhancing intramedullary cervical lesion is suspected to represent a tumor. Intraoperative findings guided the surgical procedure toward syringotomy and drainage, with tissue sampling to investigate a possible underlying neoplasm. Multilevel laminoplasty provided posterior access while allowing reconstruction of the cervical laminar elements. Histopathological confirmation and longer-term follow-up remain necessary.
tags: Cervical syringomyelia; Chiari malformation; intramedullary spinal cord lesion; laminoplasty; syringotomy; duraplasty; diagnostic dilemma.
items.title: Multilevel Cervical Laminoplasty and Syringotomy for a Long-Segment Cervical Syrinx Mimicking an Intramedullary Tumor: A Case Report

items.summary: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity through selective lookup, but the full embedding table must remain available for every possible input. We introduce Conditional Program (CP), a compressed representation that reconstructs only the rows an input requests. CP represents each row by a short code and a local scale, with a reconstruction program shared across the table. We instantiate this representation with a Gaussian trellis, norm restoration and independently decodable row records. CP's two-bit code lowers output KL by 41--63\% relative to 2-bit round-to-nearest. Analysis across three trained n-gram memory families shows that Gaussian-like coordinate statistics coexist with learned relationships among rows; at matched storage budgets, the shared trellis outperforms the fitted codebooks and low-rank residual variants we test. For DeepSeek, it reduces table storage from 203GB to 51GB, leaving room for larger workloads when the table is kept on GPU.
items.title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models

items.summary: Agents are increasingly interacting with other agents that act for different principals (people or organizations on whose behalf they work), such as a buyer's personal agent negotiating with an enterprise's seller agent. In such agent-to-agent (A2A) scenarios, each agent has its own environment and holds information and authority that the other cannot see. Moreover, the interests of each agent may be aligned (cooperative), partly aligned (mixed-motive), or opposed (competitive). Existing multi-agent system failure studies assume one orchestrator, shared workspace, or single principal. We ask how A2A systems fail when these assumptions are removed. We study more than 2,500 recorded runs of A2A systems built from different agent harnesses and models, spanning 488 scenarios across eight families (legal, CRM, security, commerce, etc.). From these traces, we derive $A^2$-Failures, a taxonomy of 20 A2A failure modes in four categories: (i) discovery and delegation, (ii) grounding and record consistency, (iii) verification, and (iv) conduct and fidelity. Three findings hold across every harness, model, and scenario studied: (1) discovery and interaction are driven by the phrasing of the task rather than the availability of peer agents; (2) no agent verifies a peer's factual claim on its own initiative, so an A2A system inherits the reliability of its least reliable participant unless the protocol or mechanism performs the check; and (3) the aggregate outcome score credits the agent completing the task while staying blind to the coordination, verification, and conduct failures beneath it, so A2A systems must be evaluated per agent, against each agent's own principal. We release the run logs behind the taxonomy at https://huggingface.co/datasets/a2a-salesforce/a2-failures.
items.title: Why Do Agent Teams Fail Across Boundaries? A Failure Taxonomy for Agent-to-Agent Systems with Private States

items.summary: Multi-agent systems promise a new axis for scaling inference: rather than having one agent think longer or sample more attempts, a task is split across many agents that work in parallel and coordinate. However, in practice, more agents can easily produce duplicate work, coordination failures, and higher costs. We therefore formulate team design as a compute allocation problem: starting from a solo agent, where should additional inference compute go to reach the reward-cost Pareto frontier? We build a minimal multi-agent harness from the ground up and trace this frontier by varying, one at a time, the workflow stage at which a lead delegates to its workers (planning, implementation, or verification), the models that form the team, and the number of workers. On ProgramBench, teams outperform solo agents but cost three to seven times as much. With the right compute allocation, however, a heterogeneous 17-agent team comes within 1.4 points of a strong homogeneous 5-agent team at 70% lower cost. This efficiency stems from three findings. First, planning is the most valuable use of workers: in a homogeneous team whose lead decides how many workers to spawn, a lead that delegates only planning to its workers, and then implements and verifies the code itself, matches the reward of a lead that delegates to workers throughout planning, implementation, and verification, at half the cost. Second, cheap models pay off as planners but not as implementers: a strong lead with cheap planners recovers 47.5% of the reward gain of an all-strong team for only 13.9% of its additional cost, whereas cheap implementers lower reward. Third, planners keep improving reward as the team grows, whereas implementers and verifiers plateau beyond four workers. Together, our results offer a guide to spending an agent budget where it counts, given the task, cost, and latency constraints a user has.
items.title: Scaling Inference-Time Compute with Teams of Coding Agents

items.summary: The Mathematics of 3D Printing Slicing: STL Geometry, Ray-Casting & Toolpaths is an open-access engineering monograph and interactive instructional module published by the Prep4Uni.Online OER Initiative . This work provides an analytical, undergraduate/postgraduate-level treatment of the computational geometry foundations required to translate three-dimensional surface meshes into layer-by-layer machine toolpaths. Aligned with international accreditation standards—specifically the Washington Accord (WA1–WA5) and EUR-ACE First/Second Cycle frameworks—this publication establishes the mathematical proofs, vector algorithms, and point-in-polygon logic governing modern additive manufacturing slicing software. Core Mathematical & Computational Themes: STL Topology & Facet Representation: Analysis of unstructured triangulated surface meshes, outward unit normal vectors (\(\mathbf{n}\)), vertex coordinate systems, and planar boundary extraction. Parametric Facet-Plane Intersection: Step-by-step vector linear interpolation for deriving the intersection segment \(S_k\) formed by cutting planes at \(z = z_k\), addressing non-manifold edges, vertex touching, and numerical epsilon shifts. Jordan Curve Theorem & Parity Logic: Formal implementation of the 2D Ray-Casting algorithm and Even-Odd Parity test for robust interior, exterior, and internal void classification across arbitrary closed slices. Toolpath Trajectory Generation: Comparative kinematics and geometry between continuous concentric perimeter offset loops and 45° zigzag parallel hatch raster patterns. Formative Assessment Suite: A three-tier verification suite comprising 8 foundational concepts, 7 real-world slicer failure debugging scenarios, and 6 step-by-step quantitative engineering worked examples. Note: The full interactive web edition—featuring client-side HTML5 simulation canvas engines, dynamic parameter sliders, and real-time slice projection mathematics—is accessible at: https://prep4uni.online/stem/physical-technologies/industrial-and-manufacturing-technologies/additive-manufacturing-3d-printing/mathematics-of-slicing/
items.title: The Mathematics of 3D Printing Slicing: STL Geometry, Ray-Casting & Toolpaths

items.summary: AUTONOMOUS NANOROBOTIC NAVIGATION AND MISSION OBSERVABILITY AT THE LIMIT First-Generation Research Flagship 01 | NANO/MICRO ROBOTICS, POWER & MISSION ENDURANCE Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli This research atlas asks a difficult engineering question: when low-Reynolds-number microfluidic flows, Brownian orientation noise, boundary adhesion, external field actuation and incomplete sensing all influence a micro/nanorobot, what would justify calling its behavior autonomous navigation rather than externally assisted motion? The volume treats navigation as an auditable, bounded mission instead of an attractive trajectory. It develops a five-layer program spanning stochastic hydrodynamics, instrument and actuation provenance, uncertainty-calibrated belief-state estimation, blinded microfluidic challenges and independent requalification. Thirty linked mathematical stations differentiate physical relations, information-theoretic functionals and proposed navigation utility measures, with assumptions, dimensions and possible falsifiers. Eighty-two research chapters each open with a core mathematical relation, followed by five independent single-page research sections. Two hundred detailed Research Gates describe decisive comparisons, confounding explanations, evidence requirements, failure conditions and successor handoff artifacts. Thirty-three provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos offer revisionable research prototypes rather than predetermined conclusions. The key comparator is an equal-budget experiment: fixed-field sequences, microscope-assisted manual control, externally tracked predictive control and candidate fused navigation are evaluated under matched total energy, information access, geometry, time, collision limits and recovery obligations. The manuscript emphasizes blind targets, flow reversal, sensor dropouts, wall adhesion, correlated observations, full-system power accounting, censored failures and post-mission retrieval. A mission arriving at its target but leaving an unrecovered device is not counted as a fully closed success. This work is a hypothesis-generating Research Atlas v1.0, not an experimental report or a validated medical technology. External magnetic, acoustic, optical and microscope infrastructure must be disclosed; no in-vivo or clinical competence is inferred from bench-top movement. Foundational DOI-linked literature provides context, not proof of the proposed integrated system. Every major claim is designed to be revised, rejected or reconstructed by a successor team using raw evidence and pre-registered falsification rules. items.summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Even agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. Beyond propagation, reward hacking can bias task routing toward reward-hacking agents and survive candidate aggregation. As potential mitigations, we evaluate code review by the coder or a separate verifier, both of which reduce delivered hacks. Together, these results establish reward hacking as a transmissible strategy whose effects extend beyond the agent in which it first emerges.

This English-language research atlas converts cargo-delivery and micromanipulation demonstrations into a falsifiable end-to-end mission-integrity problem. Eighty-two chapters each have a dedicated core-equation opening and five separate research sections. Two hundred Research Gates propose independent comparisons, physical perturbations, competing explanations, measurable failure criteria and reproducibility artifacts. Thirty-three provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos outline candidate systems that future investigators are invited to overturn, repair or rebuild. A machine-readable research atlas and formula-gate-DOI index enable AI-assisted comparison and future research reuse. items.summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
items.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention

items.summary: Long-horizon multi-agent collaboration requires memory that preserves both successful actions and the coordination structure underlying them. Existing memory systems support information sharing or procedural reuse, but often leave the evolution of shared procedures disconnected from the task dependencies and execution states of collaborating agents. This coupling also limits the direct transfer of procedural memory designed for individual agents to team settings. We propose Self-Evolving Procedural Memory (SEPM), a framework that uses task dependency graphs as a common representation for online coordination and procedural memory evolution. During execution, a lightweight shared blackboard records structured evidence alongside task dependencies, supporting the detection of goal, plan, and world-state divergence and evidence-based realignment. After execution, verified actions and dependencies are distilled into reusable procedures, while recurring failures inform warnings and constraints. The shared procedure pool evolves through creation, refinement, specialization, and retirement, guided by success and cost utility and constrained by evidence and safety requirements. Together, these mechanisms preserve the collaborative structure and applicability conditions needed to reuse experience across tasks. Evaluations on ALFWorld, WebArena, and OfficeBench under AutoGen and DyLAN show that SEPM achieves the highest task scores among the compared methods in all six benchmark settings. Under AutoGen, it improves task scores over the no-added-memory baseline by 29.85, 25.86, and 13.00 percentage points, respectively. The codebase is available at https://github.com/cookieApril/SEPM.
items.title: SEPM: Self-Evolving Procedural Memory Grounded in Task Graphs for Multi-Agent Collaboration

items.summary: We have presented a mathematically closed, comprehensive foundation for the C861 discrete spectral benchmark. Furthermore, the spectral interlacing analysis of the CN → PN structural homotopy equips the scientific machine learning community with a tool to distinguish authentic topological sensitivity from numerical discretization artifacts.
items.title: Exact Discrete Spectral Invariants as a Falsification Baseline for Learned Operator

items.summary: Multi-agent path finding (MAPF) solvers are evaluated on the schedules they produce, not on how well those schedules can be executed. Specifically, continuous-time optimal solvers can achieve even lower cost than their discrete counterparts by scheduling agents with near-zero temporal/spatial separation, and by exploiting graphs with higher connectedness; however, such schedules may prove hard to execute under a realistic controller. We integrate AOC-CBS, an anytime-optimal continuous-time MAPF solver, into a fleet coordination framework in which each agent tracks its timed path using model predictive control, and we evaluate the resulting system on congested MovingAI benchmark instances with 21 to 40 agents. Without intervention, only a fraction of the instances complete execution. We then apply T-robustness by adding a time-margin, i.e., a minimum temporal gap between agents at shared locations, as well as spatial inflation of the agent footprint. Increasing either margin raises execution success, for a relatively small increase in the schedule's sum-of-costs; it also improves how closely agents adhere to the schedule: when tracking each agent's position throughout execution and comparing it against the position it should occupy according to the schedule, the mean discrepancy falls significantly as the margin increases. In general, the two margins have different effects; temporal margin decreases deviation, giving the controller room to stay on schedule. Spatial margin affects deviation less and instead increases the clearance between agents, so that the same deviation no longer leads to a blocking stall. They are nonetheless substitutes rather than complements: spatial inflation is almost free in schedule cost, but its effect on execution success is small and does not compound with a temporal margin already in place.
items.title: The Cost of Executability: Temporal Margins for Continuous-Time Multi-Agent Path Finding under Closed-Loop Control

items.summary: Safe multi-agent coordination typically assumes what real-world, deployed, resource-constrained robots cannot provide: continuous, perfect state sharing. Robust control strategies must be complemented with robust communication strategies to deliver resilient deployments. In this work, we propose a unified control/communication strategy that provides safe control to guarantee inter-agent safety under intermittent communication and demonstrate its effectiveness in a pursuit-evasion scenario. Each agent computes the reachable set of neighboring agents based on the last state information received, then solves for a safe control input based on control barrier functions to ensure agents avoid collision. We prove that inter-agent collision avoidance is guaranteed provided communication staleness remains bounded. As the reachable set inflates between state transmissions, each agent reasons about when to preemptively transmit its state information to neighboring agents based on novel metrics characterizing uncertainty risk and kinematic risk. We implement and simulate a variety of pursuit-evasion scenarios and show that preemptive communication reduces messages by 77.5% compared to periodic and event-triggered baselines with zero collisions.
items.title: Robust Multi-Agent Pursuit with Preemptive Communication via Reachability-Based Control Barrier Functions

items.summary: Chlorine-based disinfectants are standard for environmental-surface disinfection in healthcare facilities, yet their reaction with organic residues generates disinfection by-products (DBPs) whose occurrence, levels, and occupational relevance on hospital surfaces remain uncharacterized. Key gaps are the lack of a validated method and baseline data, the unresolved origin of surface N-nitrosamines, and the unknown influence of chlorine, temperature, humidity, and pre-cleaning on the surface DBP signal. We developed an isotope-dilution wipe-sampling, solid-phase extraction, and ultra-performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) method for eight priority DBPs, applied it to 125 wipe samples from five departments across three campuses of a tertiary hospital in Wenzhou, and complemented field work with stainless-steel coupon experiments. Validation gave r ≥ 0.999, detection limits of 0.8–3.8 pg/cm², and recoveries of 78.4%–96.8%; field detection and quantification frequencies were 87.2% (95% CI 80.2–92.0%) and 69.6% (95% CI 61.1–77.0%), with operating rooms showing the highest total load (Kruskal–Wallis H(4) = 27.86, P < 0.001) though no pairwise contrast survived Bonferroni correction. In coupon experiments the net signal rose with chlorine and temperature but not humidity, with an unexplained chlorine-dependent increment (≈55% at 2000 mg/L) reflecting analytical signal behavior rather than verified formation chemistry, and pre-cleaning reduced haloacetic acids and chlorophenols by 35–55% but N-nitrosamines by only 3–9%. These results provide the first isotope-dilution baseline of DBP loads on healthcare surfaces, a reproducible monitoring method, and occurrence data for revising disinfection and occupational-hygiene standards, and they identify precursor-controlled formation experiments, biological monitoring, and direct testing of medical rubber as next steps.
tags: disinfection by-products; healthcare environmental surface; ultra-performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry; wipe sampling; N-nitrosamines; occupational exposure
items.title: Determination of Chlorination Disinfection By-products on Healthcare Environmental Surfaces by Ultra-Performance Liquid Chromatography–Tandem Mass Spectrometry

Experiments across reasoning, coding, and executable agent environments demonstrate that RCM outperforms strong centralized and decentralized coordination baselines by up to 18.7 points in task performance and 10.2 points in Responsibility, while improving failure and harm detection without task-specific training.
items.title: A Responsibility-Centered Coordination Mechanism for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Medical prescribing errors for multimorbid patients, who require complex drug regimens, are a major patient safety concern. These errors often stem from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties, a critical coordination failure that leads to adverse drug events and rehospitalizations. To address this coordination challenge, we introduce PRISMATIC, a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents, each representing a workflow role, collaboratively generate and refine treatment plans. Operating on a blackboard architecture, the system first structures patient information from clinical notes, then iteratively develops safe, rational, and interpretable drug regimens. The agents' collaboration is governed by two novel adaptive coordination mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (DSWA), a long-term mechanism that adjusts the influence weights of agents based on historical case outcomes, enabling the system to adapt and trust more reliable specialists over time. (2) Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (DFPC), a short-term mechanism where agents provide iterative feedback to resolve disagreements and eliminate prescription conflicts for the current patient. Experiments on patient records from the MIMIC-IV database show that PRISMATIC significantly reduces drug conflicts, improves prescription coverage, and enhances treatment consistency compared to strong LLM baselines. Our work demonstrates that structuring clinical co-treatment as a multi-agent coordination problem offers a promising path toward safer and more coherent multidisease management.
items.title: PRISMATIC : Prescription Risk Inspection System for Multi-Agent Treatment Interaction in Clinical Decision-Making

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a Structured PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23431625 . Does the introduction explain the objective of the research presented in the preprint? Yes The introduction clearly explains the research objectives. It states that the study aims to replicate the quantitative analysis of Krause, Krause, and Bränfors (2018), assess the reproducibility of their findings, and examine potential limitations concerning statistical power and model specification. Are the methods well-suited for this research? Somewhat appropriate The replication approach is suitable for the research, as the authors reproduce the original Cox proportional hazards models and robustness tests. However, the methodological assessment has some gaps. In particular, the power analysis reports values of 0.44 and 0.99 without providing the formula, software procedure, or sufficient calculation details to allow readers to reproduce the estimates. The choice of 42 events in Table 6 also needs clarification, given that Table 5 reports 54 events overall. Additionally, the differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes remain unexplained. These issues weaken the transparency and reproducibility of the analysis. Are the conclusions supported by the data? Somewhat supported The main conclusion is that the original findings can be reproduced, which is supported by the reported results. The authors also reasonably identify the small number of female-signatory agreements and the limitations of drawing causal conclusions from the observed association. However, the claim that the analysis has low statistical power relies on a calculation for which the formula and detailed procedure are not provided (Table 6). The differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes also remain unexplained. These limitations make some aspects of the interpretation less conclusive than they could be. Are the data presentations, including visualizations, well-suited to represent the data? Somewhat appropriate and clear The survival analysis and regression tables are suitable for presenting the findings. However, some numerical inconsistencies in the descriptive statistics and differences in sample sizes across the original and reproduced models need clarification to ensure the results are presented accurately. For instance, Table 3 presents: three major statistical flaws: 1: Conflict Intensity row, where Female Signatories = 1: has SD of 1.2 while the Max is 0.45, which is statistically incorrect. Similarly, (2) Democracy row where Female Signatories = 1, has Mean 0.92 < Min 1. And lastly, on page 5, UN peacekeeping is written as a binary number, however, in Table 3, the binary UN Peacekeeping has Max > 1. All these minor inconsistencies require clarification. How clearly do the authors discuss, explain, and interpret their findings and potential next steps for the research? Very clearly The authors explain their findings, acknowledge the limitations of the small number of agreements with female signatories, and discuss the implications for causal interpretation. They also identify the need for further research, although the power analysis and differences in sample sizes could be explained more transparently. Is the preprint likely to advance academic knowledge? Somewhat likely If the author clarified the sample-size discrepancies and documented the power analysis more transparently, then it would substantially contribute to the reproducibility of an influential finding, as it already highlights the reproducibility of the findings and highlights the limitations in statistical power and causal interpretation. items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23432006 . The paper (arXiv 2610.21914) is a pre-registered study of 465 merged agent-authored pull requests from 246 repositories (Sections 3.2-3.5). A frozen pipeline of four review agents and one fix agent ran every PR with three LLMs, and one mixed model per LLM tests CodeHealth against log total tokens (Sections 3.6-3.9). Each CodeHealth point goes with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost (Section 4.2, Table 8), but adding the size of the scored files absorbs the coefficient (Section 4.6.4, Table 15). I liked the handling of the pre-registration: the disclosure that review sessions started before filing, the amendment with a full re-collection of the 67 affected PRs (Section 3.12), and the file-size refit that weakens your own headline. I read it as a practitioner who runs coding agents every day. In my company the software development is done by AI agents, so maybe my practical side is useful here. Four comments. 1. On heavy tails (Sections 3.9, 4.2) - you note that one pilot PR was about 45% of a tier's mean token total, while in the main collection no PR exceeded 8.2% of a tier's token sum. In my measurement of 722 agent sessions (150,902 model calls, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216), about 3% of sessions gave 80% of the modeled cost. Sessions longer than 200 calls (8% of sessions) gave more than 90% of the money. So in my data the average is driven by a thin tail. What share of each LLM's tokens comes from the top 10% of PRs, and does the CodeHealth slope hold without them? 2. On cache and price (Section 3.8, Table 4, Section 6.3) - the outcome is input plus output tokens, with cached input recorded separately. In the same 722 sessions, more than 85% of the modeled cost was work with context (cache reads and cache writes). In a separate run of 168 sessions, 94.4% of billed tokens were re-reading context already sent (contextburn, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22712985). That is a share of tokens, not of the bill, because cached reads are the cheapest tokens. So a raw token total and a bill can rank PRs differently. Could you refit H1 with cached input priced at each provider's cache-read rate? 3. On paging long files (Sections 3.6, 5.2, 3.13) - the paper links the extra iterations to the 500-line limit per read call. In my guides I write that quality drops as the agent's context fills, and that heavy reading should go to a subagent so the main conversation stays clean. Since tool results are appended to the message history (Section 3.6), paging the median unhealthy-tier file of 2,146 lines puts every page into history that is re-sent on every later call. From the session records, can you count file-read calls and repeat reads of the same file per tier? That would test the paging explanation directly. 4. On the cost of what (Sections 5.5, 5.6, 6.3) - the study does not assess whether comments are correct or fixes are good. In my guides I write that every task needs its own check the agent can run. Without it, "looks done" is the only signal the agent has. I also use a second, fresh agent whose job is to refute the first one, because AI sounds equally sure when it is right and when it is wrong. For the 27-PR replication subsample (Section 3.11), you could run the repository tests after the fix and have a fresh agent try to refute each comment. Tokens per surviving finding would be a cheap first step toward Section 5.6. Thank you for a clear and useful paper. Competing interests Yes: the text cites the author's own technical reports (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216, 10.5281/zenodo.22712985); no connection to the article's authors. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) The author declares that they used generative AI to come up with new ideas for their review.
items.title: PREreview of "CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests"

items.summary: Data Type: CSV, Experiment  Organized by: Research group of Shenzhen Research Institute, University of International Business and Economics, and a principal researcher from the University of Sassari, Italy  Approval ID: UIBE-4635876 The dataset contains 876 linked scene records representing 73 participants, each contributing responses to 12 virtual tourism presentations. Six destination settings are represented: a heritage courtyard, coastal promenade, forest trail, museum gallery, mountain lookout and historic street. Each setting has a LiDAR and a photogrammetric version, yielding 438 records per reconstruction condition. Each row identifies a participant, destination and reconstruction condition. The source CSV contains participant age and VR familiarity, presentation order, exposure duration, experiential ratings and technical descriptors. Experiential variables include psychological immersion, presence, perceived spatial coherence, emotional valence, arousal and workload. Technical variables include geometric error, texture ratings, frame rate, motion summaries and the interval between modality sessions. Neural features comprise 1,200 EEG values organised across 30 channels and 40 frequency bins spanning 1–40 Hz, together with 12 fMRI regional summaries. The regional labels cover bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal, precentral, postcentral, inferior parietal and superior parietal regions, plus ventromedial prefrontal cortex and precuneus. These values use arbitrary units and do not represent raw electrical waveforms or anatomically extracted BOLD measurements. The analysis CSV aggregates EEG frequency values into five bands: delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma. This produces 150 EEG features per record. Combining these with the 12 regional summaries produces 162 neural predictors. Mean immersion combines the two session ratings; values of at least 4.5 define the high immersion category. The analysis file also contains participant validation fold assignments, held-out predictions and classifier scores. All records from a participant share the same validation fold. Prediction and score columns are analytical outputs and must be excluded from model inputs. Mean immersion is 4.59 for LiDAR and 3.95 for photogrammetry. Verified primary balanced accuracy is 81.97% for EEG, 79.66% for fMRI and 79.01% for the combined model.
items.title: Decoding Immersive VR Tourism: Reconstruction Quality and Neural Indicators of Immersion

items.summary: Експертна методика визначає стадії та операції дослідження, однак сама їх послідовність іще не пояснює, за яких умов результатом однієї операції можна скористатися в наступній. У судовій гірничотехнічній експертизі найбільш відповідальними є переходи від відомостей, що їх містять матеріали, до реконструкції механізму події, від реконструкції – до оцінювання причинного значення обставин, а від установленої дії або бездіяльності – до її технічного співвіднесення з функціями конкретної особи. Мета роботи полягає у формуванні критеріїв, за якими придатність проміжного результату перевіряють до його застосування в наступній операції, та у з’ясуванні зв’язку між фактичною основою – сукупністю достатніх, узгоджених і простежуваних відомостей – і допустимими межами підсумкової відповіді експерта. Дослідження поєднало структурне моделювання, формально-логічний аналіз експертного міркування, зіставлення з положеннями судової експертології та теоретико-методичне узагальнення професійного досвіду у сфері судової гірничотехнічної експертизи. Застосування моделі проілюстровано на двох знеособлених типізованих ситуаціях із завершеної експертної практики 2015–2023 років, що відображають різний стан фактичної основи. Обґрунтовано поняття критерію контрольованого переходу й сім функціональних контрольних точок: відповідності питання компетенції експерта; достатності матеріалів; узгодженості та простежуваності відомостей; можливості реконструкції механізму; причинного значення обставин; суб’єктно-функціонального співвіднесення; синтезу й оцінювання результатів. Для фіксації методичного рішення запропоновано статуси контрольованого переходу: Т+ – дозволений перехід, Т± – обмежено дозволений перехід, Т– – недозволений перехід. Практичними результатами є модель проходження контрольної точки, матриця методичних рішень і структура робочої карти, придатні для використання як методичний модуль судової гірничотехнічної експертизи. Застосування критеріїв контрольованого переходу пов’язує стан фактичної основи з допустимим напрямом подальшого аналізу й запобігає формулюванню відповіді поза обумовленими межами.
items.title: Критерії контрольованого переходу між операціями судово-експертного дослідження як засіб забезпечення обґрунтованості висновку в судовій гірничотехнічній експертизі
